summary: Specifies ways to use the Arcfour cipher in the Secure Shell protocol that reduce the weakness of the cipher's key-scheduling algorithm. It was a standards-track document, but it is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines two SSH modes that discard the beginning of an Arcfour encryption stream. It also explains that discarding those bytes does not remove every known weakness.

questions: how many arcfour keystream bytes are discarded
subtitle: Two SSH Arcfour modes that skip the cipher's weak initial keystream bytes.

tldr.problem: Arcfour, also known as RC4, has weaknesses in its key-scheduling behavior, especially near the start of its keystream.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines arcfour128 and arcfour256. Both discard the first 1536 keystream bytes and use the next byte to encrypt the first packet byte.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4345 is Historic. The RFC still warns that attacks can use later portions of the keystream and recommends against Arcfour for high-volume password-authenticated connections.

today: RFC 4345 is marked Historic in the unit metadata. It specifies improved Arcfour modes for SSH and describes remaining security limitations.

sections.title: Why Change Arcfour Use
sections.content:
SSH supports symmetric ciphers to protect data in transit. Its base protocol included Arcfour, also called RC4, a fast stream cipher. The cited SSH specification warns that Arcfour has problems with weak keys and should be used with caution.

Research cited by this RFC recommends discarding the first 1536 bytes of keystream so the cipher's internal state is more thoroughly mixed. RFC 4345 defines SSH algorithms that follow that recommendation.
sections.plainLanguage: Arcfour can produce weak output at the start of its stream. This RFC changes where SSH begins using that output.

sections.title: The Two Arcfour Modes
sections.content:
arcfour128 uses Arcfour with a 128-bit key. arcfour256 uses the same cipher with a 256-bit key. For both, implementations MUST discard the first 1536 bytes of keystream, and the first encrypted packet byte MUST use byte 1537.

The RFC says Arcfour implementations are typically somewhat faster and much smaller than other SSH encryption algorithms then defined. It recommends the algorithms in RFC 4344 in most cases where speed and code size are not critical.
sections.plainLanguage: Both modes skip the first 1536 bytes. One uses a 128-bit key and the other a 256-bit key.

sections.title: Limits of the Improvement
sections.content:
The discarded keystream bytes MUST remain secret and MUST NOT be transmitted, because their contents could reveal information about the key. The RFC distinguishes attacks on the start of a stream from attacks that can use any part of a stream.

It warns that some attacks can combine data from different streams. Repeatedly encrypting the same data, such as a password, in separate Arcfour streams could reveal information. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS that Arcfour not be used for high-volume password-authenticated connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping the beginning addresses one weakness, but attacks can still use later output and compare separate streams. The RFC advises against high-volume password connections.
